title: Home
text:
Welcome to my portfolio for MUSA 5080: Public Policy Analytics at the University of Pennsylvania.
This site documents my work in the Master of Urban Spatial Analytics program — weekly notes, course assignments, and a final project applying data analysis to urban policy questions.



 I am a student in the MUSA program at Penn. I have a background in Geography and GIS in Planning, and I am interested in communicating geographical spatial analysis for public use.
I graduated from the University of Oxford with a BA Geography in 2026. During my undergraduate studies, I focused on both the theoretical concepts of human geography and the technical skills of quantitative GIS through the lens of transportation planning.





Weekly Notes — what I’m learning each week
Assignments — analyses completed for the course
About — more background and how to reach me

title: Week 2: Getting Ready
text:
File Management
Coding Anxiety
Git & Workflow

We use R for the statistical analysis, and Quarto is used to run the code and weave the output into the final document.

Things to Note
This is to test the nesting feature on .md



Markdown is a file format that we will use to write explanations and narrative next. There is a Markdown language guide on Canvas that is common to anything that uses Markdown (.md), including Quarto.





What is the relationship between Quarto and R?


Quarto is a separate package that calls on r to run code and then builds the document around the results.


What is the difference in scope between _quarto.yml and the YAML header at the top of an individual .qmd file?


_quarto.yml adjusts the global theme settings, while the YAML header adjusts the individual header controls.


What does Git do?


It is a version tracker that runs locally on your computer, watching your folder for changes.


What is the sequence of work?


Save, Render, Commit, Push

title: Week 2: Getting Ready
text:
Objects, Verbs, Census






TipBreaking Down R Code





result <- filter(counties, population > 50000) # keep the big ones!




result - this is an object
<- - this can also be =, it is an assignment arrow
filter - this is a function
counties - this is input data
population > 50000 - this is an argument







TipPackages





Packages are things that can be installed and called upon when you are running your code




install.packages("dplyr") - this only needs to be done once
library(dplyr) - this is like a book. You need to run this every time you use r


Data Frames



Name
Income
MOE




12
12
12


123
123
123


1
1
1




Note: tibble is nicer and prints prettier
Note[2]: MOE stands for Margin of Error



Verbs

filter() - picks Rows
select() - picks Columns
mutate() - adds a new Computed Column
arrange() - change order of rows in ascending or descending order
group_by() + summarize() - many rows become few. For example, for a dataframe with many states and income levels, it can group it by state and it can summarize the income levels.



Manipulating the Data (Example - Novice)






TipStep 1





filler(counties, moe_pct >10)









TipStep 2





arrange(Step1, desc(moe_pct))









TipStep 3





Select(Step2,NAME, (moe_pct)




However, this is a very novice way of doing things because it creates more unnecessary data frames that pollute your workspace



Thinking of Advanced Ways






Tip





While it is good to think about the step-by-step process to be clear about how you are manipulating the data, you can start using the % code to string together functions to compute your data output without creating the files in between.




For Example
New__Data <- Counties %>% 
  filter(moe_pct > 10) %>% 
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  Select(NAME, moepct)






Warning



Take note that everything is case sensitive in R. A good rule of thumb is to put everything in lowercase.





The Census






TipThe Census





The census is a great source of data that we will use. It is mandated by the constitution to count the number of people that live there on an interval of every 10 years (Decennial Census, created by James Madison). Every person that is in the US (legally or illegally) is asked 10 questions on a 10 year basis.









TipAmerican Community Survey (ACS)





Created in 2005. It replaced the long form of the Decennial Census. It has more data that we are interested in (things like income, travel patterns). Roughly 3% of households are surveyed. From the sample, an estimate for the population is derived. There are two versions of the ACS.




The 1-year ACS: Only for places with >65,000 people (metropolitan level). While it is the most current, we don’t often use it in our analysis because we don’t often get the neighborhood level.
The 3-year ACS (now deprecated): not in use
The 5-year ACS: Goes down to block group, census tract…etc. This means that when you get ACS data for the year 2016 (for example), you are accessing the 5-year average of the neighborhood.


tidycensus






Tiptidycensus



tidycensus is where you can access the census through r in a simple way



It is formatted as such: B19013_001E


B is the base table
191032 is the table number
001E is the line number
E is the estimate of the MOE



Census Tracts

They are organised from State > County > Tract

A tract is a ‘neighborhood’ or around 5-8,000 people. However, the boundaries keep changing. This is why there are longtitudinal tracts like NHGIS (University of Minnesota) or LTDB (Brown University) that help combat this issue.






Warning



There are also things called block groups, but they are very unreliable. They are not representative, and you should not use this.




GEOID






Tip



It used to be an identifier. This is how you decode it.



Sample GEOID

4210100001001


42 - State
101 - County
000100 - Tract
1 - Block Group







Tip



These numbers are stored in strings. You need to keep the GEOID as a string to keep the 0s at the beginning of the first nine GEOIDS (for states that begin with A)








Warning



90% of joining issues are because of type errors between strings and numbers for the GEOID that will result in a failed join.


data <- get_acs(geography = "county",
  variables = c("B19013_001",
                "B01003_001"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5")

# when we run this code, it will give it to us in a format called tidy(long). What we want is for it to be in WIDE format:

data <- get_acs(geography = "county",
  variables = c("B19013_001",
                "B01003_001"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide")

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at Median Home Value across counties in Illinois, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "IL"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25077_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)

[1] 102   5

head(county_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  GEOID NAME                       variable   estimate   moe
  <chr> <chr>                      <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>
1 17001 Adams County, Illinois     B25077_001   155900  4554
2 17003 Alexander County, Illinois B25077_001    58700 10578
3 17005 Bond County, Illinois      B25077_001   133100 13683
4 17007 Boone County, Illinois     B25077_001   198600  8350
5 17009 Brown County, Illinois     B25077_001   142200 19435
6 17011 Bureau County, Illinois    B25077_001   121900  3733


The function returned 102 rows, which matches the number of counties within Illinois

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                       estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                         <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hardin County, Illinois       91700 31269    34.1
 2 Alexander County, Illinois    58700 10578    18.0
 3 Jasper County, Illinois      122900 17070    13.9
 4 Hamilton County, Illinois    108800 15103    13.9
 5 Brown County, Illinois       142200 19435    13.7
 6 Calhoun County, Illinois     174000 21433    12.3
 7 Pulaski County, Illinois      81000  9539    11.8
 8 Massac County, Illinois      118000 13228    11.2
 9 Scott County, Illinois       101700 11145    11.0
10 Bond County, Illinois        133100 13683    10.3


Hardin County is the county with the largest margin of error relative to its estimate at 34.09924.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    49
2 Low confidence     11
3 Moderate           42


From the calculations, 49 counties fall under ‘High Confidence’, 42 counties fall under ‘Moderate’, and 11 counties fall under ‘Low Confidence’.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                       myvarE myvarM  popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 17001 Adams County, Illinois     155900   4554 65166    NA
2 17003 Alexander County, Illinois  58700  10578  5042    NA
3 17005 Bond County, Illinois      133100  13683 16627    NA
4 17007 Boone County, Illinois     198600   8350 53316    NA
5 17009 Brown County, Illinois     142200  19435  6320    NA
6 17011 Bureau County, Illinois    121900   3733 33027    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         49        240766.
2 Low confidence          11          7351.
3 Moderate                42         19387 


This table illustrates a pattern between average population and the level of confidence we have in the Median Home Value estimates. The average population of counties with high confidence was 240,766.12, while the average population of counties with low confidence was 7350.818. Counties with moderate levels of confidence had an average population of 19,387. The pattern is generally that with higher populations, the level of confidence in the data increases.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Address all three:

Which communities in your state do we know the least about? We know the least about the 11 counties with the lowest confidence levels. This would be Pope County, Bond County, Scott County, Massac County, Pulaski County, Calhoun County, Brown County, Hamilton County, Jasper County, Alexander County, and Hardin County, which had a margin of error percent range of 10.275 to 34.099. As seen in the above table, these counties also have lower average populations compared to the rest of the state.
Why? Connect the pattern to how the ACS actually works — it’s a sample, and smaller places yield smaller samples. As the ACS5 already measures a slice of the county population, smaller counties like Hardin County (with about a population of 3623) will have smaller samples that lead to higher variability in the median. With a small population, the statistical standard error increases, resulting in imprecision within the data. Hence, we can conclude that the states with the lower populations are the communities that we know the least about from the ACS5 data.
What could go wrong? Imagine a state agency allocating funding using your variable, treating every county’s number as equally certain. Who is likely to be hurt, and how? If a state agency allocates funding using the variable of median home values, there is a high probability that the ACS5 estimate of the true median of a county may be higher than the actual value. This error in the estimate may result in low confidence counties appearing wealthier than they actually are and receiving less aid than they would need, thus resulting in an inequitable provision of welfare funding.
